source.title: Unified Defense for Large Language Models against Jailbreak and Fine-Tuning Attacks in Education
source.authors: Xin Yi; Yue Li; Dong-Sheng Shi; Linlin Wang; Xiaoling Wang; Liang He

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses hidden-state cluster measurements and a feature-substitution ablation to examine whether harmfulness and refusal are represented separately. It does not apply the original difference-in-means direction ablation/addition procedure.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior work on refusal directions and discusses RV as a baseline, but does not specify that RV uses the claim's difference-in-means extraction or test the claim's stated harmless-request effect. TSSF's jailbreak and fine-tuning defense scores are not rows because they evaluate the proposed defense, not the claimed direction. The paper's reported hidden-state results and refusal-feature substitution are included for V5.
record.test_reason: Mainly a defense paper (TSSF). Its preliminary analysis (Sec. 5.1, Figs. 3–4) carries Zhao et al.'s harmfulness-vs-refusal token-position analysis into jailbreak and fine-tuning settings. Its Fig. 7 ablation swaps the instruction-token feature for the final-token feature. Both bear on V5. The RV baseline adds the original refusal direction (Arditi et al.) as a defense, but its implementation is not described and it serves only as a comparison, so it is recorded under missing, not as a verdict.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The main conclusion is that TSSF (attention realignment, layer-wise harmfulness classifier, dual routing) defends against both jailbreak and fine-tuning attacks while limiting over-refusal. The finding that harmfulness sits at the instruction token and refusal at the final token, with fine-tuning weakening the latter, is a preliminary motivation for the method, not the headline result.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes cluster tendencies at selected token positions and uses a layer-wise classifier, attention realignment, and dual routing. It does not extract or ablate/add the original single difference-in-means refusal direction.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported representation patterns vary with token position and jailbreak strategy; attention-slipping prompts such as PAIR are described as affecting harmfulness recognition. Fine-tuning condition also differs between p = 0 and p = 0.1.
record.problems: The model used for the preliminary hidden-state plots is not stated in the accompanying prose. Figure values are not tabulated and uncertainty estimates are not reported. The prose describing accepted harmful states in the ArtPrompt xpost_inst condition is internally inconsistent.
record.rows_left_out: No rows left out. Results for TSSF as a defense and its comparisons with other methods are not direct tests of the claim's refusal direction. The RV baseline is mentioned, but the paper does not state that its implementation uses the specific difference-in-means direction or test the claim's specified benign-request behavior.

untested.parts: No causal intervention on either feature, no statistics, and a single unnamed model for Figs. 3–4. Harmless prompts are not projected separately.
No ablation of a difference-in-means direction. No induction of refusal on harmless prompts with reported rates, beyond the unspecified RV baseline.
Does not test whether jailbreaks suppress the direction, or train against its ablation.
Training procedures are not varied to test whether a direction exists.

missing.what: RV baseline (Arditi et al. refusal direction applied as a defense): jailbreak ASR. Qwen3-8B average 75.97→30.43, e.g. GCG 47.13→0.29, but Cipher 99.14 and RandomSearch 100. Llama3.2-3B average 66.71→14.92; InnoSpark-7B average 77.59→40.40. XSTest benign compliance 99.6→92.8 (Qwen), 98.4→91.2 (Llama), 99.2→96.88 (InnoSpark). Layer and coefficient are not described.
missing.locator: Sec. 6.1 Baselines; Table 1, Table 2, Table B.1, Table B.2

record.verdict_notes: Tranche set to T3: it re-applies Zhao et al.'s V5 analysis in new attack settings rather than a new method on the original question. The Figs. 3–4 curves cannot be read numerically from the text. The RV results directly add the original direction and show it fails on Cipher and RandomSearch, but without implementation details they were left as missing rather than given a V1 or V3 verdict.

versions.untested_parts: No difference-in-means direction is ablated or added; no test of refusal removal, induced refusal on harmless requests, or retained general capability after that intervention.
No abliteration or other weight edit based on the refusal direction is tested.
The study evaluates jailbreak attacks but does not test whether they suppress the claim's direction or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
No test compares a single refusal direction with an affine subspace, cone, or multiple refusal directions.
The evidence concerns hidden-state cluster tendencies and safety detection in the tested models and settings; it does not establish a general, causal separation across models and tasks.
No cross-language, base-to-instruct, or other transfer test of the claimed direction.
Fine-tuning attacks are evaluated, but the study does not vary refusal-training procedures to test when a single removable direction exists.

rows.operation_detail: Replaced the harmfulness feature from the last user-instruction token with a refusal feature from the final sequence token in the safety classifier.

conditions.value: refusal feature instead of harmfulness feature
linear safety classifier

rows.measure: Safety detection and defense performance; text says the substitution causes misclassification and weaker defense.
rows.baseline: harmfulness feature from the last user-instruction token
rows.value: weaker defense; exact value not stated
rows.note: The paper presents this as evidence that the refusal feature is not interchangeable with the harmfulness feature. Model-specific numerical values are not stated in the prose.
rows.check: The value is readable from Fig. 7; it is not 'not stated'. Jailbreak ASR for TSSF vs. the w/ refusal feature variant: Qwen3-8B 11.2 vs 42.4; Llama3.2-3B 17.7 vs 26.0; InnoSpark-7B 35.6 vs 56.8. Fine-tuning ASR: 16.7 vs 34.3; 25.3 vs 62.7; 25.7 vs 59.0. This ablates the study's own classifier, so it is only indirect evidence that the two features are not interchangeable.

source_check.correct: Fig. 7 prints the values as data labels. Order is Qwen3-8B, Llama3.2-3B-Instruct, InnoSpark-7B; TSSF bar first, w/ refusal feature bar last. TSSF's labels match Tables 1, B.1 and B.2 (11.17, 17.67, 35.59). Jailbreak ASR, TSSF vs w/ refusal feature: 11.2 vs 42.4; 17.7 vs 26.0; 35.6 vs 56.8. Fine-tuning ASR: 16.7 vs 34.3; 25.3 vs 62.7; 25.7 vs 59.0. Jailbreak CR: 93.7 vs 91.4; 94.5 vs 93.9; 96.3 vs 95.5.
source_check.locator_found: Sec. 6.3 'Impact of core components'; Fig. 7 data labels
source_check.problem: 'Exact value not stated' is wrong: Fig. 7 labels every bar. The prose discusses the substitution only for jailbreaks, but Fig. 7 also shows higher fine-tuning ASR.

labels.label: supports
labels.condition: ArtPrompt jailbreak and fine-tuning attacks (p=0, p=0.1); unnamed model in Figs. 3-4; classifier substitution on three models
labels.reason: Under ArtPrompt and fine-tuning, accepted harmful prompts sit with refused ones at xinst but in the acceptance cluster at xpost_inst (Sec. 5.1). Swapping in final-token features raises ASR on all three models (Fig. 7). The evidence is figure-only and correlational, and the 'refusal' centroid (mean of refused harmful prompts) mixes harm and refusal.

relation.reason: Its own Figs. 3-4 analysis and the Fig. 7 feature-substitution ablation bear on whether harm and refusal are encoded separately.

tranche.reason: Sec. 5.1 applies Zhao et al.'s centroid analysis at the instruction and post-instruction tokens to new settings (ArtPrompt/PAIR jailbreaks, fine-tuning attacks) and reports results on V5. It does not use Arditi's diff-in-means extraction or ablation. T2 is also arguable, but T3 fits better.

source_check.notes: The model behind Figs. 3-4 is never named. The layer axis runs 0-35, but Sec. 5.1 shows Llama-3 template tokens. The Arditi RV baseline is not a row: on Qwen3-8B it cuts average jailbreak ASR from 75.97 to 30.43 (Cipher and RandomSearch stay near 100) and lowers XSTest CR from 99.60 to 92.80 (Tables 1-2). The only text addressed to a reader is a model-response example (App. C), not an instruction.

statements.problem: For this study the claims are right: ArtPrompt and fine-tuning p=0/0.1, an unnamed model in Figs. 3-4, three named models in the classifier substitution, and correlational. Small point: the 'capability check' (XSTest, AlpacaEval, MT-Bench, FTA) evaluates the TSSF defense, not the harm/refusal analysis.

For this study it is right: under PAIR, accepted and refused harmful prompts both sit in the acceptance cluster at xinst (figure-only, unnamed model). The authors attribute this to attention slipping as PAIR lengthens prompts.
For this study it is right: Sec. 5.1 says ArtPrompt keeps the harm read at xinst, while PAIR 'often fails' to identify harmful inputs.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Hidden-state comparisons at xinst and xpost_inst in the reported jailbreak and fine-tuning analyses; feature substitution in the safety classifier
reader_labels.reason: The study reports different cluster tendencies by token position and says substituting the final-token refusal feature for the user-instruction harmfulness feature causes misclassification and weaker defense (r1, r3, r5, r6, r7, r8, r9). The ArtPrompt xpost_inst result is unclear (r2), and PAIR xpost_inst is not textually interpreted (r4).
